Hi Dad,

Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Can a computer tell from your voice that you have been drinking? Speaking takes more than a hundred muscles, and alcohol affects every one of them. The answer is at the end of this email.

  • A researcher says China’s best AI models carry traces of American chips that China is not supposed to get. The US restricts sales to China of the most powerful AI chips, made by Nvidia. A former OpenAI researcher, Will DePue, has published a report saying that six new models from four Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, carry numerical “fingerprints” of exactly these chips: the random numbers a model is filled with before training are laid out differently on different chips, and some of them survive. He himself stresses that this does not show where the chips were or whether a law was broken, since Chinese firms can rent computers abroad. Nobody independent has confirmed the finding yet. Read more and the background.
  • Four nonprofit groups ask a California court to freeze the development of more powerful AI. Anthropic is among the defendants. Four American nonprofit groups, among them the long-established consumer organisation Public Citizen, have sued Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI arm in San Francisco. They ask the court to freeze the development of ever more powerful AI, arguing that the companies themselves warn of catastrophe and that today’s systems have already slipped out of control in tests. The court has decided nothing yet, and the legal route is untested. Anthropic is a defendant; it makes Claude, which writes this email, so I only report what the documents say. Read more and the background.
  • ChatGPT gets a wallet: the AI can now pay for your shopping, but only after your fingerprint. OpenAI has begun letting ChatGPT pay for purchases: you add a bank card once, the assistant finds the goods and goes through the checkout itself. For now this is only for some US subscribers, and every purchase must be approved with a fingerprint or face; the shop and the assistant never see the real card number. Later OpenAI wants to let the assistant buy on its own within a set limit, and that is the riskier step. Meanwhile many shops and airlines still refuse to admit such assistants. Read more and the background.
  • SoftBank loses billions on power-plant equipment it ordered for AI data centers. The Japanese group SoftBank, one of OpenAI’s main backers, has reported a quarterly loss of $7.1 billion, and more than half of it comes from power-plant equipment. Data centers for AI need so much electricity that builders put up their own gas power plants, and the turbines for them are scarce. SoftBank reportedly paid non-refundable deposits on far more turbines than it needed, and now counts much of that money as lost. I read only TechCrunch’s account, not the company’s own report. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Reports: demand for Anthropic’s shares is six times the supply, and buyers from China are being turned away, OpenAI starts selling AI that hunts for security holes in companies’ software, Survey: most US state and city governments now use AI, and their workers’ unions are asking for rules.

Answer to the question of the day. Partly, and not yet reliably. Speech uses more than a hundred muscles, so alcohol changes it noticeably, the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok explains. In 2011 German researchers recorded 162 volunteers aged 21 to 64, each of them sober and after drinking, as they read numbers and tongue-twisters and simply chatted. One thing stood out: after alcohol the voice became higher, especially in women. But no single “fingerprint” of drunkenness turned up, because people’s voices differ far more from one another than one person’s voice differs before and after a drink. Italian researchers recently found a way round this. They built a program in three parts: the first picks out features of speech such as pitch, rhythm and pauses, the second decides “sober or not”, and the third tries to guess who is speaking. Whenever the third part guesses right, the first is penalised, so the program gradually learns to ignore what is personal about a voice and to keep only what alcohol changes. On people it had never heard, it was right about 71% of the time. That is better than tossing a coin, but far from a breathalyser, and the recordings were made in quiet rooms and only in German. The authors call it a step, not a finished device. Sistemny Blok, “The neural-network breathalyser: how your speech can give you away” (March 2026) (article in Russian).
